```bash
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} /api/$v/me\n" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    "https://api.target.example/api/$v/me"
done
curl -s -H "X-API-Version: 1" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://api.target.example/api/me
# 4. forged public URLs from share-token-shaped columns
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "https://target.example/index.php/s/rkNCkcYcbGEBDQN"
```
Diff four security-relevant behaviours between the mobile-era version and the current one: **auth
strength** (does the old path accept a token the new one rejects?), **rate limiting** (burst both; a
missing 429 means throttling was never backported), **input validation** (same payload to both), and
**field exposure** (does the old path return internal ids or PII the current version redacts?).
items.proof:
The same request against both versions, side by side, with the security regression visible in
the response bodies. **A version difference alone is Informational — the weakened control is the
finding.** For the share-token case, an unauthenticated 200 from a machine that never touched the device.
items.escalation:
This is where a locally-scoped provider read becomes an AM-01 remote finding, and where
the chapter's ceiling actually gets reached. -> D15 for the full API sweep, -> D13 for session handling.
Note the adjacent mobile-auth inversions when you get there: a client-side-only rate limit the API never
enforces is a real finding; an OAuth `client_secret` embedded in the app is never-submit, whereas **PKCE
non-enforcement** is the reportable one.
items.ruled_out_when:
Every identifier in the provider is device-local (a row id, a local cache key) and the
extracted token is rejected off-device with a 401 that a valid token does not produce — show both the
401 and a control 200.

items.title: The Downloads provider and the signed URL that outlives the session
items.vrt: `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.pii_leakage_exposure` (varies); `sensitive_data_exposure.disclosure_of_secrets.for_publicly_accessible_asset` (P1) if the signed URL is replayable by anyone
items.maps_to: `reference/android/app/DownloadManager` — `Request.setDestinationInExternalPublicDir()`, `Request.addRequestHeader()`, `COLUMN_LOCAL_URI`, `Request.setVisibleInDownloadsUi()`
items.test:
Three questions, not one. Where does the downloaded document rest, is the download URL (with its
query-string token) readable through the Downloads provider, and does `setVisibleInDownloadsUi(true)`
expose a private document in the system Downloads UI. `addRequestHeader()` also attaches the app's
`Authorization` header to the download, which is how signed URLs end up in a world-readable row.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'DownloadManager|setDestinationInExternalPublicDir|setDestinationUri|addRequestHeader|setVisibleInDownloadsUi|allowScanningByMediaScanner' "$DEC/jadx/sources/"
# after downloading an in-app document (invoice, statement, KYC copy, chat attachment):
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell ls -la /sdcard/Download/
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell "content query --uri content://downloads/my_downloads \
  --projection \"_id,uri,local_uri,title,status,notificationpackage\""
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell content query --uri content://downloads/all_downloads
```
items.proof:
Either `ls -la` showing a per-user document readable outside the sandbox, **or** a
`content://downloads/my_downloads` row whose `uri` contains `?token=`/`?sig=`/`X-Amz-Signature` that still
returns 200 when replayed with `curl` from another machine. Replay it off-device — that is what separates
metadata disclosure from a real finding.
items.escalation:
-> D07-070 (the signed URL is a backend credential); the public download directory is also
a **write** target, so chain it to the app's own import routine (D07-064).
items.ruled_out_when:
Downloads go to `setDestinationInExternalFilesDir` (app-scoped) or an internal path,
and the provider row's `uri` column either is absent or returns 401/403 on off-device replay.

items.title: MediaStore cross-owner read and `OWNER_PACKAGE_NAME` redaction
items.applies_to: Scoped storage from Android 10 (API 29); `requestLegacyExternalStorage` ignored at targetSdk 30+; `READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` has no effect from Android 13 (API 33); `OWNER_PACKAGE_NAME` redaction from Android 14
items.maps_to: MASTG-KNOW-0042, MASTG-TEST-0202, MASTG-TEST-0254, MASTG-TOOL-0004; `about/versions/14/behavior-changes-all` (`OWNER_PACKAGE_NAME` redaction, `QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES`)
items.test:
Two questions. (a) Can the app read media belonging to other apps, and does it hold
`MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` to do so? (b) Does the app use `OWNER_PACKAGE_NAME` as a **provenance** check
("this file came from a trusted app, so skip validation")? From Android 14 that column is redacted unless
the owner is always-visible or the caller holds `QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES` — so a trust branch keyed on it now
fails open on attacker-supplied media.
items.how:
```bash
grep -nE 'MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE|READ_MEDIA_IMAGES|READ_MEDIA_VIDEO|READ_MEDIA_AUDIO|READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED' "$DEC/apktool/AndroidManifest.xml"
grep -rn 'OWNER_PACKAGE_NAME' "$DEC/jadx/sources/"
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell content query --uri content://media/external_primary/images/media
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell content query --uri content://media/external_primary/file
# then place a file from a third app and observe which branch the target takes
```
items.proof:
For (a): the **absence** of
`java.lang.SecurityException: com.target.app has no access to content://media/external_primary/images/media/<id>`
on a cross-owner read, or `MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` held with no justification in the store listing.
For (b): a Frida hook on `Cursor.getString` logging a null/redacted owner value while the trust branch
still executes.
items.escalation:
-> D17 (a malicious file trusted because of provenance reaches a parser); -> D20 for the
bulk-media case. Broad file access plus a WebView `file://` primitive -> D10.
items.ruled_out_when:
The app reads only its own attributed media (every cross-owner probe throws the
`no access` SecurityException), does not hold `MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE`, and makes no authorisation
decision on `OWNER_PACKAGE_NAME`.

items.title: `androidx.startup` and other fixed-authority providers — install-time authority collision (documented, low impact)
items.vrt: `application_level_denial_of_service_dos` (varies) — availability only; see the doctrine note below
items.applies_to: apps using AndroidX App Startup or any fixed-authority initialiser
items.maps_to: `topic/libraries/app-startup` (authority format `${applicationId}.androidx-startup`, `android:exported="false"`); `PackageManager.INSTALL_FAILED_CONFLICTING_PROVIDER` — the installer refuses a package whose authority is already registered ("Can't install because provider name X (in package Y) is already used by Z"). Documented; the experiment is for the evidence line, not for the fact.
items.test:
Android refuses to install a package whose provider authority is already claimed by an installed
package (`INSTALL_FAILED_CONFLICTING_PROVIDER`). An attacker app that pre-registers
`com.target.app.androidx-startup` prevents the legitimate app from installing (a distribution denial, or a
forced sideload/downgrade), or is itself rejected if installed second — a one-way install DoS rather than
a data bug. Impact is pre-installation only (the victim app is normally already installed); report only to
programmes that buy availability, as Low.
items.how:
```bash
# 1. install an attacker app declaring the target's startup authority
#    <provider android:name=".Stub" android:authorities="com.target.app.androidx-startup"
#              android:exported="false"/>
adb -s "$SERIAL" install attacker-authority.apk
# 2. attempt to install the target
adb -s "$SERIAL" install target.apk
# 3. observe
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell dumpsys package providers | grep androidx-startup
```
Refuted if step 2 succeeds; confirmed if it fails with a conflicting-provider error.
items.proof:
The exact installer output from step 2 (e.g. `INSTALL_FAILED_CONFLICTING_PROVIDER`), plus the
`dumpsys` line showing which package holds the authority. Nothing less.
items.escalation:
None directly. Report only with the observed installer output, and only to a programme
that buys availability findings — most do not.
items.ruled_out_when:
Step 2 installs successfully, or the app declares no fixed-authority provider outside
its own `applicationId` namespace. Record the installer output either way.

items.title: Evidence package for a provider finding
items.maps_to: the five-screenshot state-change pattern; HAR/transcript sanitising and the PII split (mask the secret, leave the correlation data visible); `docs/04-poc-and-evidence-standard.md`
items.test:
A provider read needs the bytes; a provider **write** needs a state change, and a state change
needs five artefacts, not one. Capture them in one sitting — re-running the app between captures
regenerates state and invalidates the earlier ones.
items.how:
For a write finding, in this order, named
`{finding-#}-step{n}-{description}.png` and referenced by filename in the body:
1. **Pre-state** — `content query` showing the row before, with your marker absent
   (`grep -c "$M" baseline.txt` = 0, per D07-050).
2. **The bug** — the `content insert`/`update`/`call` succeeding from an app UID with no permissions.
   The most important artefact.
3. **Post-state negative** — the old value no longer present.
4. **Post-state positive** — the new value present, marker visible.
5. **Side effect** — the app's UI or the backend reflecting the change, or the absence of any
   notification to the user (which proves whether a passive defence exists).

Sanitising, ranked by practicality: (A) do not capture the secret at all — screenshot the row with the
token column projected out, and keep the full capture locally for the triager via the platform's private
attachment system, never email; (B) black-bar in an image editor; (C) find/replace on transcripts:
```bash
sed -E 's/(access_token|refresh_token|Authorization|password|pin)=[^,[:space:]]+/\1=<REDACTED>/g' \
  provider_dump.txt > provider_dump.sanitised.txt
grep -iE 'token|password|bearer' provider_dump.sanitised.txt | head   # verify
```
**Leave visible** — the triager needs them: the authority and URI, your own attacker uid/package, the
column *names*, request/trace ids, the exact exception strings, and the `Required Permission - Read: null`
line. **Mask** — token values, password hashes, other users' PII, the device's IMEI/serial.
items.proof:
Five numbered cross-referenced artefacts plus a sanitised transcript, with the unredacted
originals retained locally. After submission, rotate the test account's credentials so anything visible in
a screenshot is already dead.
items.escalation: n/a.
items.ruled_out_when: n/a — unconditional for every write or state-change finding in this domain.

items.title: Pre-severity gate against the Critical claim, not against the bug
items.applies_to: every D07 Critical or High claim
items.maps_to: the Pre-Severity Gate and retraction discipline; `docs/02-severity-and-reportability.md`
items.test:
Write the draft Critical title, then substitute the **Critical claim** — not the bug — into each
question. This domain generates confirmed primitives that do not complete a chain more than any other,
because a provider read is genuinely exciting and genuinely often ends at a value the backend rejects.
1. Have I validated the full chain to attacker-attainable impact, or only one primitive? "Traversal
   confirmed" is not "account takeover".
2. What does the attacker walk away with, in one concrete sentence?
3. Have I personally reproduced the full chain end to end at least twice — once on discovery, once for
   the PoC — and from an **app UID** both times (D07-007)?
4. Is there still a gate? A token that is device-bound, a refresh that requires an attestation, a file
   that is encrypted with a Keystore key you cannot use off-device. If yes, it is "primitive present" at
   a lower severity, documented honestly.
5. Has the programme rejected this class before? Nextcloud's published carve-out for same-device apps is
   the standing example — check it before, not after.
items.how:
Record the five answers in the working notes before drafting. For anything Critical or High,
reproduce through **two independent stacks**: `adb shell content` and a PoC app's `ContentResolver`, or
drozer and a PoC app. Cross-tool consistency rules out tool artefacts.
items.proof: The five answers plus two independent reproductions in the report.
items.escalation:
When a claim fails the gate, downgrade it and write the retraction into the appendix
rather than silently dropping it:
```markdown
### Retracted: <finding name>
- **Original signal:** <what looked like a bug>
- **Disproving evidence:** <reproduction step + observation>
- **Why it looked like a bug:** <marker collision / shell-UID artefact / status-only confidence>
- **Retraction date:** <YYYY-MM-DD>
```
The inverse rule matters just as much here: **do not retract a confirmed finding that stopped
reproducing because the client patched mid-engagement.** Keep the timestamped pre-patch `content query`
output — providers are easy to fix quietly, and a same-day patch is common.
items.ruled_out_when: n/a — unconditional for every Critical/High in this chapter.

items.title: Chain-filing order for provider primitives
items.applies_to: every D07 finding that feeds another domain
items.maps_to: chain-filing order: primitives first so their ids exist, then the consumer, then backfill the links; "one fix equals one bounty" — a chain is a severity amplifier, not a merge request
items.test:
D07 is a primitive factory: the traversal, the over-broad paths XML, the grant configuration and
the injection each have **independent fix surfaces**, and each becomes Critical only in combination with
a consumer in D08, D15 or D17. Filing them as one giant report loses money and confuses triage; filing
them without cross-references loses the severity.
items.how:
1. Identify the highest-severity chained outcome (usually "token theft -> ATO" or "arbitrary write ->
   code execution").
2. File each primitive separately at its standalone severity, with a placeholder cross-reference line:
   e.g. the FileProvider `<root-path>` config (D07-057), the redirector that issues the grant (D08), the
   loader that executes the written file (D17).
3. File the chain consumer with the full narrative at the chained severity, filling in the real primitive
   ids.
4. Edit each primitive to backfill the consumer's id.
```markdown
## Chain partners (filed as separate reports)
- **submission [UUID-1]** — FileProvider `<root-path path="."/>` exposes the app data directory
- **submission [UUID-2]** — `ShareActivity` forwards an attacker Intent with FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION
These primitives have independent fix surfaces and are filed separately per the programme's
"one fix = one bounty" rule.
```
items.proof:
Cross-referenced submissions. Do not paste the whole chain narrative into every primitive, do
not claim each primitive is independently Critical, and do not ask for a single combined bounty.
items.escalation:
Open the severity request in the consumer's first body section, naming the VRT node you
chose and the priority you are asking for, with the reachability proof as the reasoning.
items.ruled_out_when: n/a — mechanics; every D07 primitive that feeds another domain is filed in this order.

items.title: Provider probe contract — positive control, full verb matrix, exception text
items.applies_to: every app-UID provider probe in this chapter (D07-005, D07-010, D07-018, D07-019, D07-078)
items.maps_to: MASTG-TECH-0148 (the `content` command runs as `shell`); the D07-006 layer table; `attacker-app/README.md` (`provider` step)
items.record: logs/D07-077.txt (the full `PROBE` log of one run, control line included); the pulled `files/probe-<session>.log` mirror; inventory/components.csv `notes`
items.skip_when: n/a — unconditional for every app-UID provider negative.
items.test:
A provider negative is only as good as the probe that produced it. The probe must (1) log
`Throwable.toString()` — class **and** message — never `getClass().getSimpleName()`, because the layer
classification in D07-006 is made on the message; (2) run the full overridable surface per authority —
`query`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`, `bulkInsert`, `applyBatch`, `call` (every name from D07-017),
`openFile` r/w, `openAssetFile`, `openTypedAssetFile`, `getType`, `getStreamTypes`, `canonicalize`,
`refresh` — not `query` plus a few `call()` names; (3) carry a **positive control**: a known-readable
authority is queried first in the same run, so a run with zero positives is proven to be a result and not
a dead harness; (4) declare `<queries>` per D07-008; (5) be started with `am start -S` so `onCreate` runs
on every launch, with a distinct action per fire in a loop. The shared probe app does all five; a
per-engagement rewrite that drops one of them manufactures false negatives for the whole domain.
items.how:
Use the shared probe (`attacker-app/`, `provider` step); if it lacks a verb, add it there rather
than building a per-engagement copy.
```bash
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell am start -S -n com.sanehunters.probe/.MainActivity --es run provider --es victim "$PKG" \
  --es authority "$AUTH" --es methods "<call() names from D07-017>"      # verbs default to all 18
adb -s "$SERIAL" logcat -d -s PROBE:V | tee logs/D07-077.txt
adb -s "$SERIAL" pull /sdcard/Android/data/com.sanehunters.probe/files/ logs/probe/   # the file mirror; some builds drop app Log.i
grep -c 'POSITIVE CONTROL' logs/D07-077.txt     # must be 1 — otherwise every zero in the run is UNVERIFIED
```
items.proof:
The control authority returning rows in the same log as the target results; one line per
authority per verb with the full exception text (`java.lang.SecurityException: Permission Denial: ...`),
and the `ready` line showing `requestedPermissions=[]`.
items.escalation:
Feeds the D07-005 / D07-010 / D07-018 / D07-019 tables; a verb that returns a value where
`query` was denied reopens the authority (D07-015, D07-018).
items.ruled_out_when:
n/a — unconditional. A provider negative recorded from a probe without a positive
control, or without the exception message, is an unfinished test, not a ruled-out row.

items.title: `getType()` reaches non-exported providers through the system-server MIME path
items.applies_to: every provider, exported or not, whose `getType()` or `getTypeAnonymous()` override does more than return a constant
items.maps_to: MASTG-TECH-0148; AOSP `ContentProvider.getTypeAnonymous()` javadoc (API 34: "does not need to be permission protected")
items.record: logs/D07-078.txt (probe log for the oldest and the newest API in the lab, with the API level in the header)
items.skip_when: `grep -rnE 'String (getType|getTypeAnonymous)\(' "$DEC/jadx/sources"` shows no override outside framework packages → notes: "no provider overrides getType/getTypeAnonymous (grep count 0)".
items.test:
When the caller cannot acquire the provider, `ContentResolver.getType()` asks the system server,
which resolves the MIME type with system identity. On Android 13 and below that executes the provider's
own `getType(uri)` for any caller — exported or not, no permission. From Android 14 the unpermitted path
is routed to `getTypeAnonymous(uri)` (framework default `null`) and only permitted callers reach
`getType()`. An override that performs a path or database lookup is therefore a row-existence oracle and
a code path that executes inside a non-exported provider: on API <= 33 (inside most `minSdk` ranges)
always, on 14+ wherever `getTypeAnonymous` is overridden.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'public String (getType|getTypeAnonymous)\(' "$DEC/jadx/sources" -A15
```
From the probe (zero permissions; this path needs no `<queries>` entry — note whether one was declared
anyway), run the `getType` verb against an id that exists, an id that does not, and a nonsense path, on
the lowest API image inside `minSdk` and on the newest:
```bash
adb -s "$SERIAL" shell am start -S -n com.sanehunters.probe/.MainActivity --es run provider --es victim "$PKG" \
  --es authority "$AUTH" --es verbs getType --es paths "/items/1,/items/999999,/nonexistent"
adb -s "$SERIAL" logcat -d -s PROBE:V | grep 'verb=getType' | tee -a logs/D07-078.txt
```
items.proof:
A non-null MIME string (or a differing exception) returned for a provider whose `query()` on

items.title: `Bundle`-form `query()`/`insert()`/`update()`/`delete()` — the SQL sinks the CLI cannot send
items.applies_to: providers overriding `query(Uri, String[], Bundle, CancellationSignal)` (API 26+) or `insert/update/delete(..., Bundle)` (API 30+)
items.maps_to: MASTG-TEST-0339, MASTG-TECH-0148, MASTG-BEST-0039
items.record: logs/D07-079.txt (probe log with the Bundle keys sent and the parser error or row-count pair)
items.skip_when: the grep below is empty → notes: "no Bundle-form provider override (grep count 0); the legacy signatures are covered by D07-038..042".
items.test:
`ContentResolver.query(uri, projection, queryArgs, signal)` carries `QUERY_ARG_SQL_SELECTION`,
`QUERY_ARG_SQL_SELECTION_ARGS`, `QUERY_ARG_SQL_SORT_ORDER`, `QUERY_ARG_SQL_GROUP_BY`, `QUERY_ARG_SQL_HAVING`
and `QUERY_ARG_SQL_LIMIT`. The framework's default Bundle-form `query()` forwards only selection, args and
sort order to the legacy signature, but a provider that overrides the Bundle form reads GROUP BY, HAVING
and LIMIT and splices them into `SQLiteQueryBuilder.query(...)` or a raw string. `adb -s "$SERIAL" shell content` has
no flag for any of them, so a full CLI sweep (D07-038..042) says nothing about these three sinks, and the
write overloads with a `Bundle extras` argument are a fourth path the CLI never exercises.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'QUERY_ARG_SQL_(GROUP_BY|HAVING|LIMIT|SELECTION)|public Cursor query\(Uri [a-z]+, String\[\] [a-z]+, Bundle|public int (update|delete)\(Uri [a-z]+, (ContentValues [a-z]+, )?Bundle' "$DEC/jadx/sources"
```
From the probe app (add the verb to the shared probe if it is missing: a `Bundle` with one key per run,
starting with `QUERY_ARG_SQL_LIMIT` and `QUERY_ARG_SQL_GROUP_BY` set to a syntactically broken value
such as a lone single quote), against the seeded dataset from D07-049, then the same key with a valid
value — the pair is the oracle.
items.proof:
A parser error naming `GROUP BY`/`HAVING`/`LIMIT`, or a boolean row-count differential driven
only through a Bundle key, on a seeded dataset (D07-049) — recorded with the exact key and value.
items.escalation:
D07-038 (extraction through the error channel); D07-042 (the blind oracle through the
write overloads); D07-043 when `setStrict(true)` is on but the subquery form survives.
items.ruled_out_when:
No Bundle-form override exists (grep empty, file list recorded), or every key is routed
through `SQLiteQueryBuilder` with `setStrictGrammar(true)` and the probe throws `Invalid token` — proved
with the D07-044 negative control, not by reading the builder.

items.title: The app's own `DocumentsProvider` — document ids that escape the picked root
items.attacker: AM-04 (the user picks the app's root once in the system picker)
items.applies_to: apps with a class extending `DocumentsProvider` (a cloud-storage, notes or file-manager feature exposed to the Storage Access Framework)
items.maps_to: MASTG-TECH-0159; `guide/topics/providers/create-document-provider` (`isChildDocument`, `MANAGE_DOCUMENTS`)
items.skip_when: `grep -rl 'extends DocumentsProvider' "$DEC/jadx/sources"` is empty → notes: "no DocumentsProvider subclass; the SAF consumer side is D07-064".
items.test:
The provider must be exported with `android.permission.MANAGE_DOCUMENTS`, so only the system
picker calls it directly — but any app can send `ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT_TREE`, and once the user picks the
app's root the caller holds a tree grant and can mint any document URI under it with
`DocumentsContract.buildDocumentUriUsingTree(tree, id)`. `openDocument(documentId, ...)` and
`queryChildDocuments(parentId, ...)` receive that id; if ids are filesystem paths (or encode one) and
`isChildDocument(parentId, childId)` is absent or compares string prefixes, an id carrying `..` resolves
outside the picked root. D07-064 is the consumer side of SAF; this is the server side.
items.how:
```bash
grep -rnE 'extends DocumentsProvider|openDocument\(|queryChildDocuments\(|isChildDocument\(|getDocIdForFile|getFileForDocId' "$DEC/jadx/sources" -A10
```
Obtain the tree grant through the picker in a stub that sends `ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT_TREE` and persists the
returned tree URI; then open `buildDocumentUriUsingTree(tree, <rootId> + "/../../shared_prefs/x.xml")`
with `openInputStream` and log the first bytes, and `queryChildDocuments` on a parent id outside the root.
items.proof:
Bytes from outside the picked root returned under a tree grant, plus the decompiled
`isChildDocument` (or its absence) at file:line.
items.escalation: The D07-028 impact set (token files, databases); `"w"` mode -> D07-035 -> D17.
items.ruled_out_when:
`isChildDocument` canonicalises both ids (file:line) and the probe throws
`SecurityException: Document ... is not a child of ...` for the traversal id.
